newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish opposition gives Yilmaz parliamentary test.
newsitem.headline: Turkish opposition gives Yilmaz parliamentary test.

text.p: Turkey's former Islamist-led coalition parties poured scorn on the new secularist government in parliament on Thursday, saying it was doomed to collapse because it lacked popular support.
Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz's left-right coalition faced a barrage of opposition attacks on its programme at a debate ahead of a confidence vote on Saturday.

"This government is not eternal, it will certainly go," said Islam-based Welfare Party deputy Bulent Arinc in a speech. "You are scared of the people, a government without the support of the people cannot stay on its feet."
The Islamists' conservative allies in opposition reinforced the attack on the government's plans.

"The government programme is a routine, dull and lifeless document," said True Path Party deputy Ayvaz Gokdemir. "From the time it came until when it goes we will not let its (the coalition's) collar out of our hands."
Yilmaz, a conservative, has around a dozen more deputies on paper than he needs to win the vote in the 550-seat assembly.
A key leftist leader pledged his party's support for the incoming secularist coalition.
"We will support the government for the sake of Turkey," said Deniz Baykal of the Republican People's Party, whose support is essential if Yilmaz is to survive the weekend vote.
Baykal said his party, with 49 deputies, would vote for the coalition to keep the previous Islamist-led government out of power, rather than to show its support for Yilmaz.
Islamist prime minister Necmettin Erbakan resigned under army pressure last month after angering NATO-member Turkey's military with a series of symbolic challenges to the country's secular tradition.
The new government has vowed to implement an army demand for state education to be extended to eight years at the expense of religious schools.
"You are staging a coup against religious education," Arinc said.

A senior Islamist politician said Yilmaz's administration was a tool of the secularist elite. "The government doesn't have a programme of its own," former minister Abdullah Gul told a news conference.

"This government's mission was written down and handed to it," he said. The Islamists say President Suleyman Demirel, who is supposed to steer clear of party politics, helped Yilmaz to power unfairly in a closing of secularist ranks against them.

Yilmaz promised anti-Islamist measures, including the extension of secularist education, when he read out his government programme in parliament on Monday. The opposition did not have an immediate right of reply to that speech.
He also said he would speed up privatisation, despite being in partnership with a left-wing party opposed in the past to selling state assets.
The government has said it will hold early elections next year, well before polls are due in the year 2000.
